title: Strategies for LLM Evals (GuideLLM, lm-eval-harness, OpenAI Evals Workshop) — Taylor Jordan Smith

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk is primarily about evaluation design, benchmarks, and testing methodology for LLMs, covering a tiered evaluation pyramid from system performance to safety evals. The evaluation methods and frameworks discussed are not tied to any specific application vertical and apply across general AI systems. The content primarily addresses evaluation and testing of LLM systems, with secondary coverage of deployment and serving considerations for production inference. The workshop requires no prior evaluation expertise but involves hands-on model deployment, benchmarking, and custom evaluation creation. The session includes three hands-on activities with live tool usage against deployed models. Eleven direct transcript evidence anchors support the classification across multiple aspects of the talk.

summary: Taylor Smith establishes why production-grade generative AI is exceptionally difficult to deploy safely and at scale, framing evaluations as essential risk management. He describes a typical enterprise maturity path—automating tasks with AI, building chatbots, implementing RAG, and eventually adopting agents—noting most Red Hat customers remain in the first three phases. He catalogues key genAI drawbacks: corporate policy restrictions on allowable models, legal exposure from hallucinations (citing the Google AI overview glue incident), bias from eurocentric training data, high cost and performance demands, and knowledge cutoffs requiring RAG or agent-based solutions. He emphasizes inference at scale, naming production-grade runtimes like TRT-LLM, SGLang, and vLLM as necessary for real-world traffic, and details evaluation pain points including complex workload testing setup, heavy compute requirements, dataset-model compatibility, GPU resource optimization, and difficult cost estimation. Smith clarifies that evaluation is a comprehensive end-to-end assessment while benchmarking is a specific subcategory using controlled datasets and tasks for comparison (e.g., MMLU, latency scores). He introduces a tiered evaluation pyramid analogous to the software engineering testing pyramid: the base layer is system performance (throughput, latency, GPU utilization), followed by factual accuracy (MMLU benchmarks, fine-tuning accuracy), then safety, bias, and custom application-specific evaluations at the top. He recommends building evaluation capabilities incrementally—starting with unit-test-like component evaluation before expanding to integration and end-to-end testing. The workshop includes three hands-on activities that move up this pyramid. Activity 1 uses GuideLLM to benchmark system performance metrics (inter-token latency, time to first token, throughput) against a vLLM-deployed IBM Granite model. Activity 2 uses lm-eval-harness with MMLU Pro for factual accuracy benchmarking. Activity 3 uses Promptfoo for safety evaluation with customizable tests. Smith highlights that all frameworks are open source and customizable, including creating MMLU-style evaluations with proprietary datasets. During wrap-up, an audience member asks about connecting evaluations to running production use cases to track real-world performance, which Smith identifies as implementing a CI/CD framework for evaluation—analogous to automated testing in software engineering. He encourages continued use of his GitHub repository as a learning resource and offers ongoing support via a Slack channel.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Production genAI deployment is complex and risky, making robust evaluations critical for managing customer risk and company credibility.
Organizations should take an incremental maturity path: chatbot automation, then RAG, then agents—most enterprises are still in early phases.
Key genAI drawbacks include policy restrictions, legal exposure from hallucinations, training data bias, cost/performance challenges, and knowledge cutoffs.
Production inference requires purpose-built runtimes (TRT-LLM, SGLang, vLLM); traditional runtimes cannot handle real-world concurrent traffic efficiently.
Evaluation (comprehensive end-to-end assessment) and benchmarking (controlled dataset-specific comparisons) are distinct but related activities.
A tiered evaluation pyramid mirrors software testing: system performance at the base, factual accuracy in the middle, safety/bias/custom evals at the top.
The three hands-on activities move up the pyramid: GuideLLM for system performance, lm-eval-harness with MMLU Pro for factual accuracy, and Promptfoo for safety and custom evals.
Connecting evaluations to live production use cases to track real-world performance is best conceptualized as a CI/CD framework for evaluation, analogous to automated testing in software engineering.
Open-source eval frameworks are fully customizable, enabling MMLU-style evaluations with proprietary datasets and custom safety tests.
Organizations should build evaluation capabilities incrementally, starting with component-level tests before expanding to integration and end-to-end evaluation.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.summary: Taylor Smith introduces himself as a Red Hat AI developer advocate, notes this is his first time at the conference, and outlines the session: challenges of production LLM deployment, the need for evaluations and benchmarks, and planned hands-on activities with evaluation tools.

sections.title: Challenges of Production GenAI and Maturity Path
sections.summary: Smith describes setting up genAI in production as extremely complex, lists major drawbacks (policy restrictions, legal risks, bias, cost/performance, knowledge cutoffs), and outlines the typical enterprise incremental maturity path from chatbots to RAG to agents.

sections.title: Inference at Scale
sections.summary: Discusses inference bottlenecks under concurrent load, names production-grade runtimes (TRT-LLM, SGLang, vLLM), and details evaluation pain points: complex workload testing setup, compute demands, dataset-model compatibility, GPU resource optimization, and difficult cost estimation.

sections.title: AI Failure Examples and Mitigation
sections.summary: Cites stable diffusion bias, the Google AI overview glue incident from unmitigated satire, and the MAD problem of synthetic data degradation. Notes that Google and Stable Diffusion introduced additional evaluation frameworks and mitigations after these incidents.

sections.title: Evaluation vs Benchmarking Definitions
sections.summary: Clarifies that evaluation is a comprehensive end-to-end model assessment while benchmarking is a specific subcategory using controlled datasets and tasks for comparison (e.g., MMLU, latency scores). Both custom evals and benchmarks will be covered in hands-on activities.

sections.title: System-Specific and Incremental Evaluation Strategy
sections.summary: Emphasizes that evaluation setups depend on system type (Ragas for RAG, function-calling for agents), require continuous CI-like improvement, and should be built incrementally—starting with evaluating chunk retrieval in a RAG pipeline before expanding to all components.

sections.title: Evaluation Pyramid and System Performance Overview
sections.summary: Introduces a tiered evaluation pyramid mirroring the software engineering testing pyramid: base layer is system performance (throughput, latency, GPU utilization), middle is factual accuracy (MMLU, fine-tuning accuracy), top is safety, bias, and custom application-specific evals. Announces GuideLLM as the tool for the first hands-on activity on system performance benchmarking.

sections.title: Hands-On Activity 1: GuideLLM System Performance Benchmarking
sections.summary: Walks through the first hands-on activity using GuideLLM to benchmark system performance against a vLLM-deployed IBM Granite model. Covers deploying vLLM in a container, installing GuideLLM, running benchmark sweeps (inter-token latency, time to first token, throughput) at rate 5, and interpreting mean/median/P99 results. Notes vLLM's safetensor compatibility advantage over TRT-LLM, adjustable input/output token levels for different use cases, and JSON export. Mentions three activities total and confirms all frameworks are open source and customizable.

sections.title: Custom Evals, Activity 3 Setup, and Wrap-Up
sections.summary: Discusses creating custom MMLU-style evaluations with proprietary fine-tuned data by forking open-source frameworks. Encounters rendering issues with Activity 3 content and shares links via a Slack channel 'workshop beyond benchmarks.' Recaps all three activities moving up the evaluation pyramid: GuideLLM for system performance, lm-eval-harness with MMLU Pro for factual accuracy (chosen as fastest option, ~10 minutes), and Promptfoo for safety evaluation with customizable tests. An audience member asks about connecting evals to production use cases; Smith identifies this as implementing a CI/CD framework for evaluation. Environments available until approximately 5-6pm. Encourages ongoing use of GitHub repo and Slack for questions.

demonstrations: Hands-on Activity 1: Using GuideLLM to benchmark system performance (inter-token latency, time to first token, throughput) against a vLLM-deployed IBM Granite model, with adjustable input/output token levels for different use cases
Deploying vLLM inference runtime as a container with IBM Granite model, using Hugging Face token for model access
Running GuideLLM benchmark sweep at rate 5, viewing mean/median/P99 performance metrics in internal UI, with JSON export option
Hands-on Activity 2: Using lm-eval-harness with MMLU Pro for factual accuracy benchmarking (took approximately 10 minutes)

limitations: GenAI models have knowledge cutoffs due to non-continuous training, requiring RAG or agent systems for up-to-date information.
Most public internet training data is eurocentric and US-based, introducing bias into models.
Performance evaluation under enterprise-level workloads requires manual setup and heavy compute load.
Cost estimating for inference is described as 'black magic'—difficult to map performance to token costs accurately.
Closed-source AI offerings lack transparency in how they implement mitigations.
Evaluating every component of a system is time and resource intensive, making incremental approaches necessary.
L4 GPU used in workshop is inadequate for concurrent production-scale workloads.
TRT-LLM requires model format conversion, adding configuration complexity compared to vLLM.
MMLU Pro, while the fastest option in lm-eval-harness, still takes approximately 10 minutes to run.
Activity 3 content did not render properly in the workshop environment, requiring Smith to share links via Slack.
